response:
Diagnosis. The archive now identifies one clear winner family and two informative failures. Winner: cumulative (three-year) equity issuance ranked and weighted by chronic liquidity shortfall is the only signal with joint evidence (fmb −2.00, alpha −5.1%, t=−3.30, Sharpe −0.34), and industry-neutralizing the same mechanism *strengthened* the alpha to −6.7% (t=−4.65), so the effect is within-industry rather than a sector tilt. Failure 1: single-year flows produce tail-only alphas with null FMB slopes, while multi-year cumulations produce both — persistence, not amount, is what makes the interaction linear in the cross-section. Failure 2: the revenue-contraction axis gave a wrong-signed FMB (+2.23) alongside a negative alpha, the signature of a value/reversal main effect polluting the moderator, so I retire the sales-growth axis and keep liquidity/cash-burn axes. This generation therefore consolidates on the serial-dilution-under-illiquidity mechanism along three orthogonal design dimensions (net-of-buyback flow, share-count vs. cash-raised, frequency vs. amount), sharpens the distress axis to a burn *streak*, and opens two new channels on the debt and payout sides.

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Net serial equity dilution under chronic shortfall
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(sstk, prstkc), 3), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
HYPOTHESIS: Over a three-year window it is net equity extracted from shareholders, not gross issuance, that measures dependence on outside capital; illiquid firms that repeatedly take in more equity than they return are financing survival, while illiquid firms that repurchase on net are signalling genuine cash generation.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The best archive signal uses gross three-year sstk, which lumps repurchasing firms together with non-issuers at the bottom of the sort and thus wastes the informative long leg; netting out prstkc gives the financing leg genuine two-sided variation, which is precisely what the FMB slope needs while the illiquid-heavy-issuer short leg is unchanged. This is a targeted structural improvement to the one mechanism with joint cross-sectional and portfolio support, not a new story.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Share-count dilution versus cash raised
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(csho, 3)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
HYPOTHESIS: If the distressed-dilution effect works through ownership dilution and the adverse selection it reveals, then three-year growth in shares outstanding should carry the signal at least as well as dollars raised; if instead the effect works through the cash-raising transaction itself, share-count growth will be materially weaker.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: csho is an untouched financing variable in this archive and it is reported far more widely than cash-flow-statement issuance items, so this simultaneously tests the mechanism's channel and addresses the persistently low (~0.08–0.12) coverage of the winning family. Holding the chronic-liquidity-shortfall weight fixed makes the comparison with signal 1 a clean attribution test rather than a relabeling.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Issuance frequency under chronic shortfall
EXPRESSION: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(sstk, at), 0.05), 5), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
HYPOTHESIS: What identifies a firm that lives off the capital market is how often it must return, not how much it raised in any single trip; counting years with a material (>5% of assets) equity raise over five years measures habitual dependence and should predict low returns among firms without liquidity buffers.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: This isolates one design dimension relative to signals 1 and 2 — frequency versus magnitude — and a count is immune to the extreme right-skew that has repeatedly killed the FMB slope for dollar-based issuance measures. It also naturally down-weights the single large opportunistic offering by a healthy-but-illiquid firm, which is the most plausible source of noise in the winning signal's short leg.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Cumulative issuance against an operating cash-burn streak
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(oancf), 0), 3))
HYPOTHESIS: The distress state that makes repeated issuance ominous is a persistent inability to generate operating cash, not the level of cash or working capital: firms funding three consecutive years of negative operating cash flow with new equity are financing an unproven business model and underperform.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: Every version of the winning mechanism so far conditions on liquidity *stocks* (che/lct, wcap/at) or contemporaneous coverage ratios; substituting a three-year cash-burn streak tests whether the moderator should be a flow-persistence state instead, and unlike the gen-0 accounting-loss streak it uses cash rather than accruals, which explains why that earlier version gave contradictory FMB and alpha signs. Both legs are now regime measures, which should further reduce turnover and stabilize portfolio composition.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: Forced debt repayment without liquidity
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltr, at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))
HYPOTHESIS: Large gross long-term debt retirements by a firm with no cash buffer and negative working capital are not voluntary deleveraging but mandatory amortization that consumes scarce liquidity, so the same repayment that signals recovery for a liquid firm signals a funding squeeze for an illiquid one.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The archive has only tested *net* debt retirement, which conflates voluntary deleveraging with the repayment leg of a refinancing, and always with a positive expected sign; using gross dltr with a liquidity-shortfall weight tests the opposite economic reading and explains why the net-repayment signals produced solid FMB slopes but no alpha — the two subgroups have opposite return implications and cancel in the extremes.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 6---
NAME: Paying dividends while selling stock
EXPRESSION: MUL(WINSOR(MIN(RATIO(sstk, at), RATIO(dvt, at)), 2), RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
HYPOTHESIS: Simultaneously distributing cash to shareholders and raising fresh equity is internally inconsistent financing; when operating cash flow is weak relative to current liabilities, it indicates a management unwilling to cut a dividend it cannot fund and financing the shortfall by selling shares, which predicts low returns.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The MIN operator isolates exactly the overlap of the two flows, so the variable is non-zero only for the specific round-tripping configuration and cannot be reproduced by either the payout-yield or the share-issuance anomaly separately — a genuinely new interaction for this archive. Conditioning on weak cash-flow coverage supplies the distress mechanism (an unfundable dividend commitment), and this also resolves the earlier sign ambiguity about payouts under distress by testing the funding source rather than the payout level.
INTERACTION_TYPE: novel

---CRITIQUE Net serial equity dilution under chronic shortfall---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: This is a cosmetic variant of the archive's "Serial dilution with chronic cash shortfall" — identical moderator, identical 3-year window, with only prstkc netted out of the numerator — and the resulting net-equity-issuance construct is itself close to the well-known net share issuance / composite issuance anomaly.

---CRITIQUE Share-count dilution versus cash raised---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: GROWTH(csho,3) is a direct restatement of the published share-issuance/composite-issuance anomaly, and unadjusted csho growth is badly contaminated by splits and stock dividends, so the "clean attribution test" against signal 1 would be confounded by a measurement artifact rather than the economic channel.

---CRITIQUE Issuance frequency under chronic shortfall---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: Recasting issuance as a five-year count of material raises is a genuinely different design axis (habituality vs. magnitude) that plausibly fixes the right-skew problem behind the weak FMB slopes, though the five-year history requirement will likely shrink already-thin coverage and the coarse 0–5 count may produce lumpy, tie-heavy portfolio sorts.

---CRITIQUE Cumulative issuance against an operating cash-burn streak---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: Swapping the moderator from a liquidity stock to a cash-flow-persistence state is a defensible substantive change, but the proposal's diagnosis (accruals vs. cash) likely misidentifies the earlier failure — the 0/1/2/3 count multiplier reintroduces the same large mass of exact zeros that collapses the long leg and produced the contradictory FMB/alpha signs in the gen-0 loss-streak version.

---CRITIQUE Forced debt repayment without liquidity---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 4
RATIONALE: Using gross dltr rather than net retirement, with a liquidity-shortfall weight and a reversed expected sign, is a coherent and previously untested economic reading that directly rationalizes why the archive's net-deleveraging signals had slopes but no alpha; the main risk is that gross dltr proxies mechanically for debt level and short maturity structure rather than funding stress.

---CRITIQUE Paying dividends while selling stock---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: The MIN-based overlap construct is a genuinely novel interaction for this archive, but for most dividend payers sstk consists of routine option-exercise and DRIP proceeds, so the MIN will usually bind on incidental issuance rather than the deliberate round-tripping the hypothesis describes, and the surviving population may be dominated by utilities/REITs — an industry-composition risk worth an IND_RANK control.

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Burn rate against post-issuance resources
EXPRESSION: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(oancf), 0), WINSOR(RATIO(ABS(oancf), ADD(che, sstk)), 2))
HYPOTHESIS: For a firm consuming cash in operations, the relevant distress measure is how fast it burns relative to the resources it actually has after this year's fundraising: a high burn-to-resources ratio means the runway is short and another dilutive raise is imminent, which predicts low returns, whereas a firm that raised many years of burn is not under financing pressure.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: ratio
REASONING: This is not an issuance-magnitude signal at all — equity raised enters the denominator as a resource that relieves pressure, so two firms with identical issuance rank differently depending on their burn, which inverts the direction in which sstk enters relative to the entire archive and to the net-share-issuance anomaly. The indicator confines the measure to cash-burning firms, where the runway concept is economically defined, and the ratio combines a financing flow with two distress variables in a single non-separable quantity rather than a product of a financing leg and a distress weight.
INTERACTION_TYPE: ratio

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Own-history issuance peak at a liquidity trough
EXPRESSION: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(sstk, at), 5), TS_RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), 5))
HYPOTHESIS: Financing behaviour is informative relative to a firm's own norm: a firm tapping the equity market at the highest rate of its last five years precisely when its cash-to-current-liabilities position is at its five-year worst is raising capital under duress, and this within-firm coincidence predicts negative abnormal returns.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: novel
REASONING: Both legs are firm-relative percentiles rather than cross-sectional levels, so the construct is orthogonal by design to the published net-share-issuance and composite-issuance anomalies, which are level effects, and it also sidesteps the split/stock-dividend contamination that made share-count growth unusable. Economically it captures timing coincidence — the worst moment in a firm's own liquidity history is when it is issuing most — which no archive signal measures, and the bounded uniform legs keep both the FMB slope and the sorted portfolios well behaved.
